1. Introduction
Team Aquanomous is refitting an existing remote-controlled electric racing boat into a vessel
capable of autonomous operation. The original platform includes an electric propulsion system,
onboard electronics, remote-control steering and throttle, and a vision-based navigation system.
The goal of this project is to upgrade the vessel to compete in the autonomy division by
integrating systems that allow the boat to navigate and operate without direct human control. The
upgraded system includes GPS-based routing, collision avoidance sensing, controller electronics
for system coordination, and an active cooling subsystem to regulate propulsion motor
temperatures during sustained operation. These systems must work together to ensure safe
navigation, reliable propulsion, and stable operation during autonomous missions. This paper
presents the design and implementation of the autonomous vessel. It first discusses the project
objectives and background research that informed subsystem development. The paper then
reviews the design and analysis of the vessel and how the new systems integrate with the existing
platform. This is followed by an overview of the system build and subsystem implementations.
Finally, the primary risks associated with design, testing, and competition operation are
discussed along with the mitigation strategies used to ensure safe and reliable performance.

2. Objective and Background
The development of the autonomous boat required research into multiple subsystems that must
operate together to achieve reliable autonomous operation. This research focused on areas such
as control electronics, propulsion, collision avoidance systems, autonomous navigation, and
power distribution. Each subsystem plays a role in allowing the boat to navigate safely, maintain
control, and complete its mission without direct human input. Understanding how these

                                                                                                                                                   1

pages.text:
subsystems interact and support one another was important in developing a design that meets
performance, safety, and reliability requirements. The following sections summarize the
background research conducted for each subsystem and how this research influenced the design
choices used in the final system.
The development of the controller electronics subsystem for autonomous maritime vessels
involved not only work within the subsystem itself but also background research into the other
subsystems to ensure proper integration. This research focused on communication protocols,
PCB schematic design software, and relevant engineering standards. Since this vessel is an
inherited project, now requiring a fully functional and reliable autonomous navigation system,
the limitations of the existing electronics became apparent. To address this, a custom PCB was
designed and fabricated to replace the current boat electronics, improving overall system
reliability and integration. Additionally, it was realized that maintenance of the system required
significant time and careful precision to perform. To mitigate this, an IP64-rated wiring harness
system, along with detailed schematics, was developed to simplify maintenance and improve
overall system accessibility and robustness.
Background research into electric propulsion systems for small autonomous vessels showed that
higher power electric motors, such as the 48 V propulsion motor used in this system, can
generate significant heat when operating under sustained loads. While these motors can handle`
short bursts of high output, continuous operation at elevated loads can cause internal
temperatures to rise, reducing efficiency, accelerating insulation degradation, and potentially
leading to motor failure. Because the autonomous boat must operate for extended periods
without direct human monitoring, maintaining safe motor operating temperatures was identified
as an important reliability and safety requirement. To address this, an active cooling subsystem
was developed to remove heat from the motor during operation. The system uses copper tubing
wrapped around the motor housing to transfer heat away from the motor while a 12 V diaphragm
pump circulates water through the tubing. A digital temperature controller and probe monitor the
motor temperature and automatically activate the pump when a set temperature threshold is
reached. Temperature data from the probe is also transmitted to the controller electronics,
allowing the system to monitor motor conditions and activate a kill switch if the temperature
exceeds a critical limit. This provides an additional layer of protection by shutting down the
propulsion system before temperatures reach levels that could damage the motor or compromise
system reliability during autonomous operation
The autonomous navigation system has been investigated and developed by the previous two
teams working on the KY Auto Boat. Research into the system consisted of reading the previous
documentation of the components of the automation system and the software that was planned to
be used and determining if the designs were still viable. The ArduPilot firmware-based flight
controller was used with a connected companion computer, a GPS/compass module, and radio
antennas to communicate to a ground station software that can configure and write routes to the

pages.text:
flight controller. The vast majority resources for autonomous vehicles are catered to drones and
unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), but ArduPilot provides both tools that translate easily to
maritime operation and previous use cases using boats. The ArduPilot development community
is open source, has thorough documentation, is actively supported, and is used by many past and
current projects. These observations and the current work already done to develop the
automation system confirms that ArduPilot is still the ideal platform to develop the automation
system. GPS was chosen previously and was deemed to still be the most suitable way for the
craft to navigate by itself and be able to engage a kill switch to stop the navigation via a loss of
GPS. By investigating previous documentation, it was also deemed that the components and
existing system lacked in testing and verification, and in integration with the rest of the craft’s
systems. Software had been developed, but little documentation of the testing done to evaluate
the design was found, and a waterproof housing assembly for the system had not been created
yet.
A LiDAR-based collision avoidance system has been implemented to ensure the vessel operates
safely by minimizing the risk of collisions with other boats, floating debris, or any obstacles
within its path. The system utilizes carefully defined detection zones within the LiDAR sensor’s
field of view, allowing it to monitor only the most critical areas relevant to the vessel’s
trajectory. Based on the presence of objects within these zones, the sensor outputs a binary
signal, either “high” to indicate a detection or “low” to indicate that no obstacles are present. To
improve the accuracy and reliability of the system, additional filtering criteria have been
incorporated, such as minimum object size thresholds. This ensures that smaller, non-threatening
objects, which could otherwise generate unnecessary alerts, are excluded from detection. By
reducing false positives and focusing only on meaningful obstacles, the system enhances overall
situational awareness while maintaining efficient and responsive collision avoidance
performance. Furthermore, this streamlined detection approach allows for seamless integration
with higher-level control systems, enabling timely and appropriate navigational responses when
potential hazards are identified. Working closely with the autonomy subsystem, the system is
able to make informed rerouting decisions based on the location of detected obstacles, allowing
the vessel to safely navigate around them before returning to the optimal path defined by its GPS
coordinates.

When activated, the 12 V, 116 PSI pump circulates coolant through a copper tubing loop

Figure 3 - Cooling Subsystem Electronic Design Breakdown

Figure 4 illustrates the physical design of the cooling loop. The loop consists of 1/4-inch copper
tubing wrapped around the motor housing. Although the initial design specified 3/8-inch tubing,
the diameter was reduced to improve fitment and allow a longer coil length. The tubing is
wrapped more densely near the ends of the motor to avoid interference with mounting hardware
and increase thermal contact in regions of higher heat generation. A double-layer coil
configuration increases surface area and improves contact between the copper tubing and the
motor casing, enhancing conductive heat transfer.

We’re using a LiDAR-based setup to support collision avoidance by detecting and analyzing
nearby objects in real time. The current prototype operates as a standalone system, with the
sensor powered by an external battery and connected to a laptop via Ethernet for live monitoring
and data collection. This simple configuration allows us to test detection performance and
validate reliable data communication before integrating the LiDAR into the full collision
avoidance system.
The existing subsystems provide the structural, mechanical, and electrical foundation required
for the autonomous vessel platform. The BRIS inflatable hull offers sufficient buoyancy and
structural capacity to support the propulsion system, battery storage, and electronics while
remaining within the manufacturer’s motor and load ratings. The D&D electric propulsion
motor, paired with the 1268 SepEx controller, provides high torque and controllable power
delivery suitable for marine propulsion while maintaining compatibility with the 48 V power
system. The linear actuator steering mechanism enables precise control of the propulsion thrust
angle, allowing the vessel to maneuver effectively and respond to navigation commands. The
power subsystem architecture separates propulsion power from electronics power to improve
system stability and prevent electrical noise from affecting control systems. The 48 V LiFePO₄
propulsion battery bank provides approximately 4.8 kWh of energy capacity, exceeding the 55minute competition endurance requirement, while the lighter battery chemistry reduces overall
system weight compared to lead-acid alternatives, improving efficiency and vessel performance.
4. Build Overview
4.1 Controller Electronics
The final prototype of the Controller Electronics subsystem consists of a competition-ready
custom printed circuit board (PCB) integrated with the Heltec AB02S microcontroller
implementing multi-layered logic control to ensure safe maritime operation. This subsystem
contains the core control logic for both throttle and steering, with its primary role being the
integration of data from the Collision Avoidance and Autonomous Navigation subsystems. These
subsystems communicate with the Controller Electronics through direct wired connections,
allowing the Heltec microcontroller to process incoming control packets and make real-time
decisions. The subsystem is responsible for autonomously controlling throttle and steering while
simultaneously responding to obstacle avoidance commands. In addition to propulsion control,
the Controller Electronics subsystem manages the on-board electronics power distribution, as
illustrated in Figure 6. The schematic shown in Figure 6 presents the overall power flow of the
current electronics architecture and highlights the major inputs and outputs associated with the
Controller Electronics subsystem.

Figure 6: Boat Electronics Schematic
As shown in Figure 6, the subsystem utilizes two independent battery systems for operation. The primary
system for on-board electronics is a 12 V battery system, which supplies power to the linear actuator and
the microcontroller. The microcontroller voltage is stepped down from 12 V to 5 V using a DC-DC buck
converter to ensure stable operation. The second battery system is a 48 V propulsion system composed of
four 12 V batteries in series, providing a total energy capacity of approximately 4.8 kWh. This 48 V
system supplies power to the motor controller and motor. The motor power path incorporates multiple
layers of safety logic to ensure reliable and compliant operation under all conditions. The system was
tested by simulating the automation packets and testing a range of scenarios as well as invalid data points
ensuring the proper safety measures are taken to ensure safe operation.

Figure 7: Kill Switch Schematic

The motor safety logic consists of three independent layers. The first layer is the SW180
contactor solenoid, which serves as the primary means of disconnecting the 48 V supply from the
motor controller. A 350 A fuse is placed in series with the 48 V line to protect downstream
components in the event of a short circuit or high inrush transient. The second layer of logic is a
48 V relay utilizing a 3 V coil in series with a manual control switch. This configuration allows
the operator to manually enable or disable the system while also permitting electronic control via
the third logic layer. The third layer consists of an NMOS relay control circuit that connects or

pages.text:
disconnects the relay coil to ground depending on the gate voltage state. The gate signal is
controlled by the Heltec microcontroller. If the Heltec does not receive valid automation packets,
the NMOS state changes, causing the relay to open and disconnect propulsion power in
accordance with competition safety regulations. The primary components used in this control
stage include a 1 kΩ 0805 resistor, an SSM3K324RLFCT-ND NMOSFET, a TSS83L45
Schottky diode for flyback protection, and a G6C-1114P-US DC3 relay.

Figure 8: Wiring Harness Diagram

Figure 9: PCB Schematic

The custom PCB design in Figure 9 translates the previously implemented protoboard electronics
into a more permanent, robust, and competition-ready solution. The original protoboard
configuration contained several temporary wiring connections that introduced reliability
concerns. Using KiCad, the protoboard schematic was converted into a PCB layout with
improved reliability. The PCB design also includes room for future expansion, such as spare
GPIO pins routed to screw terminals for additional features or redundancy in the event of a GPIO
failure. The ground buses were consolidated into a simplified screw-terminal distribution block,
and relay connection terminals were extended to maintain compatibility with the external
auxiliary protoboard. This redesign significantly improves electrical reliability and
maintainability. A wiring harness was also implemented for ease of maintenance and
configurability for future projects with a pin out diagram illustrated in Figure 8.

The final prototype developed during this phase represents the competition-ready configuration

copper cooling loop tightly wrapped around the motor housing. Water is drawn through a basketstyle intake strainer to prevent debris or salt contamination from entering the system before being
circulated by a 12-V diaphragm pump through copper refrigerant tubing that forms a cooling
jacket around the motor casing. The copper tubing provides a high thermal conductivity path for
heat transfer away from the motor, allowing heat to be dissipated through the circulating coolant
before exiting the loop.
Thermal control of the system is managed through an onboard temperature monitoring and
feedback circuit. A waterproof temperature probe connected to an XH-W3001 digital
temperature controller monitors the motor temperature and activates the cooling pump when the
preset threshold is reached. The controller is powered from the boat’s shared 12-V power
distribution system and includes fused input and output protection to ensure electrical safety.
When the set temperature is exceeded, the controller energizes the pump through a secondary
fused output, allowing the system to automatically regulate motor temperature during operation.
All electrical components associated with the cooling subsystem are housed within a waterproof
enclosure using marine-grade wiring, sealed cable glands, heat-shrink crimp connectors, and
strain relief to ensure reliable operation in a marine environment. Figure 7 illustrates the
electrical components of the cooling system, while Figure 8 provides a detailed view of the XHW3001 temperature control module and its specifications.

Figure 12: Physical Cooling System Design Diagram

The physical plumbing layout uses 300-PSI rated fuel hose connecting the intake strainer, pump,
and copper cooling coil, with appropriate barbed fittings and hose-to-tubing adapters securing
the flow path. The copper coil is tightly wound around the motor housing to increase contact
surface area and improve heat transfer performance compared to earlier design iterations where
limited surface contact reduced cooling effectiveness. Figure 12 illustrates the physical flow path
of coolant through the cooling system components.
Preliminary validation of the subsystem has been conducted through simulation and controlled
thermal testing. Thermal modeling was used to estimate motor case temperature behavior under
representative loading conditions and evaluate system response with and without active coolant
circulation. Results indicated a measurable temperature reduction when the pump is activated,
suggesting that the selected copper coil geometry and expected coolant flow rate provide
sufficient heat transfer capability. Bench-level tests using a controlled heat source further
demonstrated that the cooling system significantly increases the rate of temperature reduction
compared to passive cooling alone.
Testing of the temperature control logic verified proper switching behavior across multiple
setpoints. The temperature controller successfully activated and deactivated the pump at
programmed thresholds, confirming that the electronic feedback system can regulate cooling
automatically during operation. Remaining work includes fabrication of the final prototype
configuration, installation on the vessel, and full validation under motor load conditions to
confirm simulated performance and refine temperature control thresholds.

Figure 13: Automation System Diagrams

Testing of the system has consisted of testing the varying the servo commands, the max distance
between base station and craft of the current radio setup for the system, and testing that the kill
switch is triggered to be engaged once GPS is lost for long enough. Varying the servo values on
the flight controller consisted of writing a mission to the flight controller, disengaging the safety
switch either manually or through a command on Mission Planner, and confirming that throttle
and steering values are being changed and set by the flight controller and being read by the Pi
accurately. Test passed. The max distance test was conducted by putting the entire automation
module into a vehicle and fixing the base station in a secure location, connecting the radios, and
recording the Mission Planner screen. It was set that the radio should be able to connect at a
distance of at least 0.25 miles, but the connection was lost within 0.1 miles. This was found to be
acceptable after learning that the PX does not need to maintain connection to the BS once the
mission has been written to follow through with navigating the route. New code was
incorporated into the Pi computer program to also parse the status of the GPS module on the PX
and send the values that means GPS is lost on the TX line if the GPS status is either missing or
getting no data. The code was run and it was seen that the GPS is lost was engaged after 3
seconds of no GPS data, and continues to operate while GPS is received on startup. It does not
try to recover and resume the mission once GPS is lost the first time.

4.4 Collision Avoidance
The current prototype for the Collision Avoidance Subsystem is configured as a standalone
LiDAR sensing setup designed to support early-stage functionality and data evaluation. In this
configuration, the LiDAR unit is powered by an external battery supply, allowing for portable
operation independent of the full craft power system. Data collected by the sensor is transmitted
to a laptop through an Ethernet connection, where it can be monitored, recorded, and analyzed in
real time. This bench-top arrangement enables preliminary testing of object detection capabilities
and sensor performance in a controlled environment prior to full system integration. The
prototype serves as an initial platform for validating LiDAR operation and establishing reliable
data communication before incorporation into the complete collision avoidance subsystem.

4.5 Existing Systems
The base platform for the vessel consists of several existing subsystems including the hull,
propulsion motor, steering system, and electrical power distribution system. The vessel is built
on a 10-ft BRIS inflatable boat hull rated for up to 10 HP, which safely supports the installed 9.1
HP electric propulsion motor and provides a total load capacity of approximately 1102 lbs for
onboard components. Propulsion is provided by a D&D DC electric motor controlled by a 1268
SepEx motor controller, which regulates motor power and speed. The propulsion circuit is
protected by a 350 A ANN fuse and SW180 solenoid kill switch to allow safe shutdown and
electrical protection. Steering is achieved using a linear actuator connected to the motor mount,
which adjusts the thrust angle of the motor to control vessel direction while providing position
feedback for accurate steering control. Electrical power is supplied through a dual-system
architecture consisting of a 48 V LiFePO₄ battery bank dedicated to the propulsion motor and a
separate 12 V LiFePO₄ battery that powers onboard electronics and sensors through a centralized
12 V distribution bus.
5. Risks
Several risks were identified during the design, construction, and operation of the cooling
subsystem. A primary design risk was insufficient heat transfer between the motor casing and the
copper cooling loop, which was mitigated by increasing coil length, tightening the wrap, and
using a double-layer configuration to improve contact and surface area. During construction,
potential coolant leaks or debris entering the system were addressed by using high-pressure rated
hose and fittings along with a basket-style intake strainer to protect the pump. Control and
electronics risks, such as inaccurate temperature readings or controller failure, were mitigated by
implementing a dedicated temperature controller, fuse protection, and waterproof housing with
marine-grade wiring. During race operation, risks such as debris ingestion, overheating, or water
exposure to electrical components are controlled through intake filtration, automatic
temperature-based pump activation, and sealed electrical connections to ensure reliable
subsystem performance.
A collision avoidance system significantly enhances the safety of our vessel by actively reducing
the likelihood of accidents on the water. By continuously monitoring the surrounding
environment, it can detect potential hazards such as nearby vessels or floating debris that may
interfere with the boat’s operation. This early detection allows for adjustments in navigation,
helping to prevent dangerous situations before they escalate. In addition to protecting the boat
from structural damage, such a system also minimizes costly repairs, and supports compliance
with maritime safety standards. Overall, it serves as a critical layer of defense in ensuring smooth
and secure operations on the water.
